items.description_text: What if sport could do more than move people? What if it could move society forward? Sport for Sustainable Development is an international Training Course bringing together youth workers, sport coaches, educators and facilitators who want to explore the potential of sport beyond physical activity. During the training, participants will discover Education Through Sport (ETS) through practice and theory and explore how sport and non-formal education can be used to address the Sustainable Development Goals, social responsibility and active citizenship. But this is not a training where you simply sit, listen and take notes. The learning process is built around experiential learning, movement, reflection, peer learning and co-creation. Participants will experience educational sport activities themselves, analyse the learning behind them and gradually build a practical toolbox of methods that can be transferred to their own organisations and communities. Working in international teams, participants will then take the next step: designing their own Education Through Sport activities connected to sustainable development, testing and improving them together, and finally facilitating them with young people at a local school. In this way, ideas developed during the training will be transformed into real educational practice. Along the way, participants will strengthen their facilitation, teamwork, communication, activity-design, reflection and leadership competences, exchange practices from different countries and build an international professional network. Grow personally and professionally. And return home ready to give something back to your organisation, your community and the young people you work with. If you believe that sport can be more than competition and want to learn how to turn movement into meaningful learning and positive change – this training course is for you! :) Infopack: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/15dvIyvNhw2gHvnZCDwcTe8O9BVGMF4tG?usp=sharing

items.description_text: Career UP – helping young people navigate career choices “Career UP” is an international training course for youth workers and other professionals working with young people in non-formal education settings. It is designed for those who want to strengthen their ability to support young people in understanding themselves, exploring career possibilities, and making realistic career decisions. Young people today face more choices, rapidly changing labour-market realities, and an overwhelming amount of information. Career UP approaches career guidance not as one final “right choice”, but as a lifelong and evolving process shaped by personal values, skills, strengths, experiences, and external factors. During the 6-day training course, participants will explore practical ways to support young people throughout this process. The programme combines non-formal education, experiential learning, reflection, peer exchange, facilitation practice, and hands-on activities. Participants will work with methods and tools that can be directly adapted to their daily work with young people. The training will focus on: supporting young people in self-understanding and self-awareness; helping them identify their values, skills, and strengths; facilitating realistic career decision-making; dealing with uncertainty, decision anxiety, and information overload; supporting young people in moving from planning to action; strengthening resilience and adaptability; using non-formal methods, facilitation techniques, and digital tools in career guidance. The training is intended for youth workers, educators, social workers, counsellors, project coordinators, mentors, community leaders, and activists. Participants should be at least 23 years old, have at least 2 years of relevant experience, be able to communicate in English, and participate in the full training course. items.description_text: The VIRTUALLYEDU Final Conference marks the culmination of the Erasmus+ project “Virtual exchanges and education on digital skills” (Project No. 101111952, Call ERASMUS-EDU-2022-VIRT-EXCH). Over the course of the project, eight partner organisations from Sweden, Armenia, Greece, Georgia and Ukraine worked together to design and test a model for delivering high-quality virtual exchange between higher education institutions and youth organisations . Join us online on 21 September 2026 to see what three years of cross-border collaboration produced. The conference brings together the consortium partners, facilitators, hackathon winners and participants of the Virtual Exchange Programme to present results, share first-hand experience and open a discussion on where virtual exchange goes next for digital inclusion, employability and online safety. What you can expect on the day: A first look at the Joint Virtual Learning & Online Collaboration Curriculum developed and piloted across the consortium, and the methodology behind the five Virtual Exchange Circles that put it into practice with real groups of students and young people. A showcase of the Digital Skills Hackathon, with winning teams presenting their projects live and sharing testimonials, plus short promo videos from the programme's cultural activities. An open panel discussion and live Q&A on virtual exchange as a tool for digital inclusion, employability and online safety - a chance to challenge the results and compare notes with practitioners from other countries. A walkthrough of the project's open-access e-learning platform and the plans in place to keep its courses and materials freely available after the project formally ends. items.description_text: Sportive Horizons is an international training activity designed for youth workers, trainers, facilitators, educators and other professionals actively involved in non-formal learning and youth work. The training explores how sport and tourism can be used as practical tools for youth development, entrepreneurship, employability and social inclusion. Rather than approaching sport only from a competitive or recreational perspective, participants will examine how sport-based and tourism-related activities can create meaningful learning experiences, develop transferable skills and encourage young people to take initiative in their communities. The programme is particularly targeted at applicants who already work, or are preparing to work, with young people through non-formal education. Participants should be interested in developing new methods that can be transferred to youth organisations, community initiatives, NGOs, sports organisations, youth centres and other environments where non-formal learning takes place. Through workshops, group work, practical activities, simulations, reflection sessions and exchange of experiences, participants will explore topics including entrepreneurship in sport and tourism, project and activity development, communication, teamwork, leadership, creativity, problem-solving and turning ideas into realistic initiatives. Particular attention will be given to understanding how these competences can be developed among young people through experiential and non-formal learning. Sport will be incorporated into the programme as an educational environment where participants can experience group dynamics, decision-making, leadership, cooperation and problem-solving in practice. Participants will explore different perspectives on democratic transformation, exchange experiences from their own countries and learn from local Polish examples and organisations working with young people and communities. items.description_text: The Training Course will explore the role of youth work in supporting the career development and empowerment of young people living in rural and smaller communities in a rapidly changing world. For many rural young people, career choices are shaped not only by fewer local opportunities, but also by deeply rooted perceptions about what is possible: “there is nothing for me here,” “to succeed I have to leave,” “entrepreneurship is for people with money or connections,” or “a good career means finding a secure job.” At the same time, digitalisation, AI, remote work and new forms of entrepreneurship are changing what it means to build a career and where opportunities can be created. YOUTH WORK CREATE will focus on the role youth work can play in challenging these limiting narratives and building a different mindset. The course approaches entrepreneurial spirit not simply as starting a business, but as a way of thinking and acting — being curious, taking initiative, recognising opportunities, solving problems, experimenting, learning from failure and having the confidence to turn ideas into action. It will also explore social entrepreneurship, encouraging young people to see challenges in their communities not only as reasons to leave, but also as opportunities to create solutions, services and positive local change. Participants will explore and test non-formal education techniques, methods and approaches for working with young people's mindsets: identifying and challenging stereotypes and limiting beliefs, discovering strengths and local resources, developing creativity and initiative, building resilience, exploring different career and entrepreneurial pathways, and moving from ideas towards action. Streetstival is a street-based youth work festival that creates space for meeting, exchanging experiences, and critically reflecting on issues that shape our work and society. Through the festival, we aim to contribute to greater recognition of street based youth work and highlight its role in building relationships, providing support, and creating spaces for young people (and others), including in places where existing systems often fail to reach them. Community is often understood as something positive and self-evident, yet not every community is necessarily inclusive, safe, or just. We therefore ask what kinds of communities we create, who they belong to, who has a place within them, and who does not. As part of the conference, the following day (Friday) we will also visit different organisations to explore good practices that contribute to community building through their work, methods and tools, and identify diverse ways in which we can contribute to building communities ourselves. Through different perspectives, we will explore questions of values, justice, inclusion, care, participation, marginalisation, and new forms of connection. We will also look at how communities are built in different spaces – from the street and the local environment to the digital world – and what role young people, youth work, and other actors play in this process. This interactive online webinar explores one of the core polarity pairs of the Polarities of Democracy framework, developed by Dr. William Benet. The session will focus on the relationship between diversity and equality, examining why both are essential for democratic societies and how balancing these values can strengthen democratic institutions, participation, and decision-making. It invites participants to slow down, return to their centre, and reconnect with the body as a place of grounding, safety and aliveness. Through embodiment, movement, authentic relating, silence and nature connection, participants explore what it means to feel at home in themselves and how to create spaces where others can experience acceptance and belonging. The journey nurtures self-awareness, emotional regulation, authentic connection and a deeper relationship with the Earth – remembering our way back to ourselves, each other and the world we belong to. A key focus of the training is belonging as an embodied experience. Participants explore what safety, acceptance and connection actually feel like in the body, and how we can return to our centre while staying open to relationship. Through nurturing practices, bodywork and shared rituals, they experience how warmth, presence and trust can allow us to become home to ourselves and to each other. The training also explores the body in relationship with the group and with nature, creating space for silence, mystery and deeper listening. Participants practice meeting themselves with greater self-love and acceptance, while developing the capacity to offer grounded, heartfelt presence and guidance to others. These experiences are translated into practical approaches for youth work, supporting participants in creating spaces where young people can feel seen, welcomed and free to be themselves. Homecoming invites youth workers to carry this sense of belonging back into their communities. items.description_text: Listening to Every Body is a six-day Erasmus+ training course exploring inclusion through emotions, body awareness, relationships and group dynamics. Together, we will look at how inclusion and exclusion are experienced at personal, group and societal levels—and how this understanding can help us create positive change in youth work. The course is designed for youth workers, trainers, facilitators, educators, project coordinators and volunteers who are actively involved in youth work and non-formal learning. We especially welcome people working directly with young people, including those facing social, cultural or economic barriers. No previous experience with the proposed methods is needed—only curiosity and a willingness to participate, reflect and learn together. The programme takes participants on a journey from the individual to the wider world. We will begin by exploring identity, emotions, inner barriers and personal patterns. From there, we will move towards group relationships, social roles, rank, privilege and collective processes, before looking at our connection with nature and the communities around us. Learning will be active and participatory. We will use movement, creative exercises, Process Work, Social Lab, Theatre of the Oppressed, group reflection, nature-based activities and the Work That Reconnects. Participants will learn through experience, exchange ideas and prepare activities that they can adapt to their own youth-work settings. By the end of the course, participants will feel better equipped to recognise exclusion and power dynamics, create more inclusive learning spaces, work constructively with emotions and group processes, and strengthen participation and belonging among young people.

items.description_text: A waiting room. A youth centre. A public square. A restroom. A courtroom. Most spaces used by young people are designed by adults. Adults decide what is needed, what feels safe and what feels welcoming. But how often do we ask young people what they think? And more importantly, how often do we invite them to create these spaces with us? The idea for this training comes from a cocreation project in which four unaccompanied minors worked with judges, guardians and children's rights experts to redesign a courtroom for the Belgian Council for Alien Law Litigation. Their ideas helped create a space that felt calmer, clearer and more respectful. The project showed that when young people are treated as equal partners, everyone benefits, including the adults who use and work in these spaces. Why does this matter? The spaces young people use every day influence how they feel, act and connect with others. When they help shape these spaces, they build confidence, ownership and a stronger sense of belonging. At the same time, the whole community can benefit from spaces that better reflect the needs and experiences of the people who use them. This training explores how youth workers can set up cocreation processes that enable young people to actively shape the spaces around them. Moving beyond participation, we focus on working together, sharing responsibility and creating solutions that reflect young people's experiences and needs. items.description_text: Storybuilders Lab: From Story to STEAM Challenge in Youth Work is a practice-based e-learning course for youth workers, youth leaders, trainers and facilitators who want to explore how storytelling, creative construction and STEAM can become tools for participation, problem solving and non-formal learning. Many STEAM activities start with a predefined outcome: build a bridge, create a vehicle, follow these instructions. Storybuilders Lab explores a different approach. The facilitator defines the learning intention, but participants influence the story, identify the problem and decide what needs to be created. The methodology follows a simple learning cycle: STORY → QUESTION → IDEAS → CHALLENGE → DESIGN → MAKE → TEST → IMPROVE → REFLECT → STORY CONTINUES Participants will learn how to use story triggers, mystery objects and open questions to generate curiosity and meaningful challenges. They will explore Story Democracy, a participatory method for collecting, combining and developing different ideas so that the direction of a project is not predetermined by the facilitator or dominated by the strongest voices in the group. A central part of the course is hands-on prototyping. Participants will work with accessible materials such as cardboard, recyclable materials and simple construction tools to turn ideas into physical prototypes. Makedo or similar cardboard-construction tools may be used where available, but no specialised equipment is required. The focus is not on creating a perfect final object. Participants practise an iterative process of: Make → Test → Notice → Change → Test again This allows them to explore how experimentation, “failure”, debugging and redesign can become valuable learning experiences in youth work. The course also addresses inclusive participation. This November, we are bringing people together from all over the world to share methods, knowledge and strategies for combating the global «care crisis» – and to develop educational formats together. Global Education Lab is an annual series of skillshare weeks for educators working on global justice, neocolonialism and global supply chains. The skillshare focuses on critical and decolonial pedagogy. It has been organised by Service Civil International since several years. About the Training Our focus this year is care and indigeneity. In a world driven by extraction and profit, the «Care Crisis» has become a global phenomenon: essential work like parenting, healthcare, and community maintenance is undervalued. This directly relates to the lack of care we give to our planet. Meanwhile, Indigenous Peoples, who safeguard 80% of the world’s remaining biodiversity, continue to face dispossession, criminalization, and the erasure of their knowledge systems. Throughout the week, participants will: Exchange knowledge on Indigenous resistance and land defence. Explore examples of environmental and Indigenous human rights defenders. Discuss alternative economic models based on the commons, reciprocity and Sumak Kawsay (Good Living). Co-create educational methods and workshop materials that connect global justice, care and Indigenous perspectives for youth education. The Lab aims to strengthen the international Global Education network while developing practical educational resources that participants can adapt and use in their own communities. An invitation to become curious about the intelligence that lives beneath our usual ways of knowing. Like mycelium moving quietly beneath the forest floor, much of what shapes us remains unseen. An invitation to tend dreams as wild and meaningful parts of ourselves. An invitation to be guided by dreams, movement, art, imagination and nature — allowing them to move with us and within us. And an invitation to explore how these practices can enrich youth work and non-formal education, creating spaces where young people can deepen their relationship with themselves, their communities and the more-than-human world. Dreaming from the Mycelium of the Earth is a 7-day Erasmus+ training course combining dreamwork, embodiment, storytelling, poetry, expressive arts, deep imagination and ecological and nature-based education. The training will offer youth workers and other professionals working with people a space to first experience these approaches themselves and then explore how they can be adapted to their own educational contexts. Throughout the programme, participants will therefore move between personal experience, group learning and professional reflection: What does this practice awaken in me? items.description_text: This course explores how youth work can become genuinely inclusive — moving beyond a declarative discourse on diversity towards everyday practice. Starting from the participants' own experience, we examine the common pitfalls that organisations, programmes and facilitators fall into (tokenism, surface-level or performative inclusion, assuming a space is neutral, one-size-fits-all approaches, accessibility treated as an afterthought, unconscious bias in recruitment and facilitation) and we build concrete solutions for designing learning and growth environments that value diversity. items.description_text: About the project Many young people spend increasing amounts of time indoors and online, while nature can be a vital source of connection, well-being and resilience. This training helps youth workers experience nature as an active part of the learning process, not just a backdrop. Participants slow down, observe, and explore their own relationship with nature — then critically reflect on what place nature holds in their youth work now, and could hold in the future. Aim & objectives The training supports youth workers in integrating nature-based learning and eco-friendly practices into their everyday work, strengthening competences in facilitation, activity design, reflection, and translating insights into practice. It follows five steps: Connect (building a safe foundation with self, others and nature), Experience (exploring nature-based methods for well-being and resilience), Critically explore (examining personal nature values and their role in practice), Design (creating activities using a practical template), and Take action (developing a concrete plan for their own work and organisation). Learning approach The training is based on Nature-Based Learning (NBL): learning in, from and about nature, spending as much time outdoors as possible. Through experiential learning — slowing down, observing, and harvesting insights — participants connect experience to practice and move toward concrete action. Central to the approach is a reciprocal relationship with nature: learning from it while exploring how this connection inspires care and responsibility.

items.description_text: Humour is already present in youth work practice - but it's rarely used as a deliberate, structured tool. "Humour is Serious Business" (HiSB) is a 6-day Erasmus+ KA153-YOU training course (27 November - 3 December 2026, Hollókő, Hungary) that will help you turn something you probably already do instinctively into an intentional, ethical, and effective competence for engaging young people. This training is aimed specifically at practitioners in the field of non-formal learning and youth work - not at the general public. You should apply if you are a youth worker (professional or voluntary), a youth leader, a young person (18+) with leadership potential already identified by your organisation, or a practitioner with relevant expertise who works with young people (e.g. a coach, mentor or tutor), even if youth work is not your primary profession. Through non-formal methods - World Café, simulations and role play, clowning and improvisation, team building, and daily reflection groups - you will explore the many different types of humour, examine cultural differences in how humour is used, reflect on your own sense of humour, and develop concrete post-programme actions to bring back to your own community. Every participant leaves with a Personal Development Plan and the chance to earn a Youthpass. HiSB is delivered by an experienced international Training Team and hosted by MAVISZ (Hungary), together with partner organisations in Poland, Portugal, Armenia, Serbia, Latvia, Croatia, Montenegro and Spain. 36 participants will take part, 4 per sending country. They will then explore how Makey Makey can be connected with Scratch and used to create interactive digital experiences such as sound installations, interactive posters, musical instruments, collaborative games, storytelling activities, art projects and team-building challenges. The STEAM approach will be embedded throughout the training: Science through conductivity, circuits and experimentation. Technology through Makey Makey and Scratch. Engineering through designing and testing interactive systems. Arts through music, storytelling, visual expression and creative design. Mathematics through sequencing, patterns, logic and problem-solving. The training is based on non-formal education principles and prioritises learning by doing, collaboration, experimentation, peer learning, reflection and active participation. items.description_text: The ENRMSC European Dialogue & Capacity-Building Forum 2027 will take place in Warsaw, Poland, in April 2027. The forum will bring together young refugees, migrants and stateless changemakers, youth workers, youth leaders, researchers, academics, civil society organisations, public institutions and other practitioners working with young people. The forum is built around a simple question: How can we move from young people being affected by systems to young people meaningfully shaping knowledge, opportunities, policies and solutions? The programme will explore meaningful participation, access to education and professional opportunities, community leadership, research and evidence, youth engagement, advocacy and collaboration between communities and institutions. Participants will take part in interactive discussions, panel sessions, workshops and facilitated group activities. The programme will combine knowledge exchange with practical capacity-building and opportunities for participants to develop new connections and potential European cooperation. A particular focus will be placed on recognising lived experience as expertise. Young refugees, migrants and stateless people will not only participate as beneficiaries but as contributors, knowledge holders, community leaders and partners in shaping discussions and recommendations. The forum will also connect participants with relevant European opportunities, networks and potential partners, including opportunities related to youth work, education, research, leadership and civic participation. The event is particularly relevant to people working in non-formal learning and youth work who engage with young people from refugee, migrant and stateless backgrounds. The guiding principle of the forum is: “Nothing About Us Without Us.” The forum is currently being developed by the European Network of Refugee, Migrant and Stateless Changemakers (ENRMSC), a refugee-, migrant- and stateless-led European civil society organisation.

items.description_text: Why this programme? Young people increasingly experience the world through digital, visual, interactive and participatory media. At the same time, heritage education can sometimes remain centred on traditional formats: guided tours, exhibitions, historical information and passive observation. This creates an opportunity for youth work. New media can provide alternative entry points into heritage, allowing young people to: explore places and stories through immersive experiences; discover hidden or forgotten narratives; connect personal and community memories with wider European heritage; question dominant interpretations of history; create their own narratives; collaborate across cultures; transform physical spaces into interactive learning environments. The programme therefore does not aim to turn youth trainers into technology specialists. Instead, it aims to help them become creative facilitators who know when, why and how to use technology to create meaningful learning experiences. General aim To strengthen the capacity of youth trainers to use new media and emerging technologies as tools for heritage awareness, intercultural learning, creativity and youth participation. Specific objectives By the end of the training, participants will be able to: Explore contemporary approaches to cultural heritage and heritage awareness. Identify opportunities for using immersive and interactive media in youth work. Experiment with VR, AR, 360° media, projection mapping, interactive installations, digital storytelling and other creative technologies. Design non-formal education activities connecting young people with local, national and European heritage. items.description_text: The project arises from a shared observation among young people, community development professionals, and partner organizations: a growing need to reconnect with the living world, rebuild social bonds, and collectively reflect on current ecological challenges in the face of the climate emergency. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition.
